subject: Science
title: Smell and taste
objectives: Children will smell safe items and say if they like the smell.
Children will taste safe foods and describe them with a word.
content: Smelling safe items, tasting safe foods, and noticing sweet, sour and salty.
teachingActivities: Check allergies and parental consent before any tasting; wash hands first; offer tiny tastes only; never force children to smell or taste; use a spoon and individual cups.
learnerActivities: Smell safe things and taste safe foods and say one word to describe them.
resources: Orange, lemon, cloves or mint leaves
Sugar, salt and a slice of lemon in small cups
assessment: Observe whether each child names a smell and says one word about how a food tastes.
expectedOutcomes: Says one word for how a food tastes.
crossCurricular: Social Habits: trying new foods politely

lessons.title: Smelling with my nose
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will smell safe items and say if they like the smell.
successCriteria: Says nice or not nice with support
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can use eyes, ears and hands to explore objects and name what they find.
resources: Orange peel, mint leaves, a bar of soap, a flower
lessons.starter: Point to your nose and say "We smell with our nose. Sniff, sniff." Smell a flower and say "Mmm."
teacherActivities: Show how to sniff gently and not breathe in hard.
Pass each pot round and say its name.
Let each child choose a favourite smell.
learnerActivities: Children sniff gently.
Children smell and say the name.
Child says yes or no with a smile or shake.
Child chooses and shows the pot.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show how to sniff gently and not breathe in hard. Children: Children sniff gently.
Step 2. Teacher: Pass each pot round and say its name. Children: Children smell and say the name.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "Do you like the smell?" Children: Child says yes or no with a smile or shake.
Step 4. Teacher: Let each child choose a favourite smell. Children: Child chooses and shows the pot.

practical.title: Smell pots
steps: Put safe items in covered pots.
Say what the smell is and if it is nice.
practical.safety: Use only safe, non-allergenic items and check for allergies first. Never use strong chemicals or cleaning products.

differentiation.support: Hold the pot at a distance and let the child sniff.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to find something at home that smells nice.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

expectedOutcomes: Says if they like a smell
lessons.conclusion: Cover the pots and say "Thank you, nose."
lessons.homeConnection: Smell flowers and foods with your child and say what you smell.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "smell safe items and say if they like the smell" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Nice and not nice smells
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will describe smells as nice or not nice.
successCriteria: Names one thing that smells nice
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can use eyes, ears and hands to explore objects and name what they find.
resources: Safe items such as an orange, mint, soap and a ripe banana
Picture cards of rubbish and flowers
lessons.starter: Hold up the orange and say "Mmm, this smells nice." Show a picture of rubbish and say "This smells not nice."
teacherActivities: Pass the items round and ask "Nice or not nice?"
Show picture cards and ask "Does it smell nice?"
Talk about why we keep rubbish away from where we eat.
Let each child choose their favourite smell.
learnerActivities: Children smell and say nice or not nice.
Child says or shows with a face.
Children listen and nod.
Child chooses and says a word.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Pass the items round and ask "Nice or not nice?" Children: Children smell and say nice or not nice.
Step 2. Teacher: Show picture cards and ask "Does it smell nice?" Children: Child says or shows with a face.
Step 3. Teacher: Talk about why we keep rubbish away from where we eat. Children: Children listen and nod.
Step 4. Teacher: Let each child choose their favourite smell. Children: Child chooses and says a word.

practical.title: Nice smells
steps: Put four safe items on a tray.
practical.safety: Use only fresh, safe items and check allergies. Never let children smell rubbish or chemicals.

differentiation.support: Offer two items and ask which one is nicer.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to name a smell they like at home.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

expectedOutcomes: Describes smells as nice or not nice
lessons.conclusion: Put the items away and say "Mmm."
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about nice smells when you cook at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "describe smells as nice or not nice" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Tasting with my tongue
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will taste safe foods and say one word to describe them.
successCriteria: Tastes a small piece of food
Says a word for the taste
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can use eyes, ears and hands to explore objects and name what they find.
resources: Small pieces of banana, orange and bread on a plate
lessons.starter: Point to your tongue and say "We taste with our tongue." Check allergy notes and wash hands together.
teacherActivities: Show each food and name it. Give a tiny piece to each child.
Ask "How does it taste?" and wait.
Wipe mouths and say thank you.
learnerActivities: Children look and take a piece.
Children chew and swallow.
Child says a word such as nice or sweet.
Child says thank you.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show each food and name it. Give a tiny piece to each child. Children: Children look and take a piece.
Step 2. Teacher: Say "Chew slowly" and show how. Children: Children chew and swallow.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "How does it taste?" and wait. Children: Child says a word such as nice or sweet.
Step 4. Teacher: Wipe mouths and say thank you. Children: Child says thank you.

practical.title: Tasting tray
steps: Each child tastes a tiny piece of each food.
practical.safety: Check every child’s allergy information first and cut food into very small pieces. Sit children down and supervise closely for choking.

differentiation.support: Offer one food and let the child lick it if they do not want to bite.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to name a food they like at home.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

expectedOutcomes: Says a word about the taste
lessons.conclusion: Wash hands and say "Thank you for the food."
lessons.homeConnection: Let your child taste small safe foods and say how they taste.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "taste safe foods and say one word to describe them" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Sweet, sour and salty
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will taste something sweet, sour and salty and match each word to its taste.
successCriteria: Matches a word to the taste with support
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can use eyes, ears and hands to explore objects and name what they find.
resources: A pinch of sugar, a drop of lemon juice and a very small pinch of salt on separate spoons
lessons.starter: Say "Today we find sweet, sour and salty." Show three small spoons.
teacherActivities: Check allergies and show each spoon and say its name.
Give a tiny taste of sugar and say "Sweet."
Give a drop of lemon and say "Sour." Do the same with salt.
Offer water and ask "Which one did you like?"
learnerActivities: Children look and listen.
Child tastes and says sweet.
Child tastes and says sour or salty.
Child says a word or points.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Check allergies and show each spoon and say its name. Children: Children look and listen.
Step 2. Teacher: Give a tiny taste of sugar and say "Sweet." Children: Child tastes and says sweet.
Step 3. Teacher: Give a drop of lemon and say "Sour." Do the same with salt. Children: Child tastes and says sour or salty.
Step 4. Teacher: Offer water and ask "Which one did you like?" Children: Child says a word or points.

practical.title: Three tastes
steps: Each child tastes sugar, lemon and salt in tiny amounts.
Match the word to the taste.
practical.safety: Use only tiny amounts and check allergies first. Do not force any child. Offer water and watch closely.

differentiation.support: Offer sweet only and let the child choose to try more.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to name a sweet and a salty food they like.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

expectedOutcomes: Names sweet, sour and salty with support
lessons.conclusion: Sip water and say "Thank you, tongue."
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about sweet, sour and salty foods at mealtimes.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "taste something sweet, sour and salty and match each word to its taste" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Week 4 smell and taste check
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Teachers will observe how each child uses smell and taste to explore.
successCriteria: Says a word about a taste
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can use eyes, ears and hands to explore objects and name what they find.
lessons.starter: Say "Nose and tongue" and show two stations.
teacherActivities: Set up two stations: smell pots and tasting.
At each station ask "What do you smell?" and "How does it taste?"
Record each child’s level and take photographs.
learnerActivities: Children rotate every six minutes.
Child answers with a word or gesture.
Children wash hands and tidy.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Set up two stations: smell pots and tasting. Children: Children rotate every six minutes.
Step 2. Teacher: At each station ask "What do you smell?" and "How does it taste?" Children: Child answers with a word or gesture.
Step 3. Teacher: Record each child’s level and take photographs. Children: Children wash hands and tidy.

practical.title: Smell and taste stations
practical.safety: Check allergies again and supervise every station closely. Cut food very small and offer water.

differentiation.support: Provide an adult partner and offer one choice.
differentiation.extension: Ask a confident child to describe a taste to a friend.

assessment.method: Observe and record Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding for: smells gently; says nice or not nice; says a word about a taste.

expectedOutcomes: Has an observation record for Week 4
Describes smells and tastes with a word
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about smells and tastes when you cook.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "Teachers will observe how each child uses smell and taste to explore" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?
